name: Thomson's Cathode Ray Experiment
statement: By deflecting cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields, Thomson found particles far lighter than any atom: the electron.
statementAccent: found particles far lighter than any atom
meaning: Thomson's cathode ray experiment was the set of experiments performed by the British physicist J. J. Thomson in 1897 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, which discovered the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified. Cathode rays are the glowing streams emitted from the negative electrode in an evacuated tube when a high voltage is applied, and their nature was disputed. Thomson studied how these rays were deflected by electric and magnetic fields. By balancing the deflection caused by an electric field against that caused by a magnetic field, he was able to measure the ratio of the electric charge to the mass of the particles making up the rays. He found this charge-to-mass ratio to be about a thousand times larger than that of the hydrogen ion, the lightest particle then known, implying that the cathode-ray particles, which he called corpuscles, were far smaller and lighter than atoms. He further found that they were the same whatever gas or electrode material he used, concluding they are a universal constituent of all matter. This showed that the atom is not indivisible but contains smaller negatively charged particles, later called electrons, and led Thomson to his plum pudding model of the atom.
mechanism: The experiment determined the nature of cathode rays by measuring how they respond to electric and magnetic forces. In an evacuated glass tube, a high voltage between two electrodes produced cathode rays travelling from the negative cathode toward the positive anode, and a narrow beam of these rays was made to strike the end of the tube, where it produced a glowing spot. Thomson passed the beam through a region where he could apply an electric field, using charged plates, and a magnetic field, using coils, arranged so their deflections opposed each other. An electric field deflects the charged particles by one amount and a magnetic field by another, and each deflection depends differently on the particles' charge, mass, and speed. By first balancing the electric and magnetic deflections so the beam went straight, he found the particles' speed, and then, from the deflection produced by the electric field alone, he could calculate the ratio of their charge to their mass. This charge-to-mass ratio came out roughly a thousand times larger than that of a hydrogen ion, meaning the particles were extraordinarily light. That the same particles appeared regardless of the cathode material or the residual gas showed they are a fundamental, universal component of matter, the electron.

variants.name: Corpuscles

variants.name: The plum pudding model
variants.text: Thomson's resulting picture of the atom as negatively charged corpuscles embedded in a sphere of positive charge.

whyItMatters: Thomson's cathode ray experiment is one of the most important experiments in the history of physics, because it discovered the electron and, with it, the first evidence that the atom is not indivisible. By showing that cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles far lighter than any atom and common to all matter, Thomson identified a fundamental subatomic particle and overturned the ancient idea of the atom as the smallest, uncuttable unit of matter. This opened the era of subatomic physics and led directly to models of atomic structure, beginning with Thomson's own plum pudding model and continuing through Rutherford's nuclear atom and the quantum theory that followed. The electron he discovered is central to chemistry, electricity, magnetism, and electronics, and the charge-to-mass ratio he measured, combined with Millikan's later measurement of the electron's charge, yielded the electron's mass. Thomson's careful method of balancing electric and magnetic deflections became a model of quantitative experimental physics, and his work earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics.

limits: Thomson's cathode ray experiment measured the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron, not its charge or mass separately, so the actual mass and charge of the electron followed only later, when Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the charge and the two results were combined. Thomson's figure for the charge-to-mass ratio implied the electron is about a thousand times lighter than the hydrogen ion, an early estimate; the modern value of the mass ratio is closer to eighteen hundred, so his round thousandfold figure was approximate. The plum pudding model he proposed was soon overturned by Rutherford's discovery of the nucleus, so Thomson's atomic model was a stepping stone, not the final picture. His 1906 Nobel Prize was cited for investigations into the conduction of electricity by gases rather than explicitly for discovering the electron.
misreadings: Thomson's cathode ray experiment did not measure the electron's mass or charge directly; it measured the charge-to-mass ratio, with the separate values coming only after Millikan measured the charge. His round thousandfold lightness was an early estimate, since the true mass ratio is nearer eighteen hundred. And his plum pudding model was not the lasting picture of the atom, being overturned by Rutherford's nucleus, so treating the experiment as weighing the electron, the thousandfold figure as exact, or the plum pudding model as final, misreads the experiment that discovered the electron.
origin: Experiments by the British physicist J. J. Thomson in 1897 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, measuring the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode-ray particles and discovering the electron, the first known subatomic particle.
